subject: english-literature
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.explain: The play was written by John Boynton Priestley, a committed socialist playwright.

questions.q: In what year is the action of the play set?
questions.explain: The play is set in 1912, two years before the First World War and just before the Titanic sank.

questions.q: In what year was the play first written and performed?
questions.explain: Priestley wrote the play in 1945, at the end of the Second World War, creating a gap of hindsight between setting and audience.

questions.q: In which fictional industrial town is the play set?
questions.explain: The action takes place in Brumley, a fictional manufacturing town in the North Midlands.

questions.q: What is the name of the inspector who calls on the Birling family?
questions.explain: Inspector Goole arrives to question the family; his name suggests 'ghoul', hinting at his mysterious nature.

questions.q: To whom is Sheila Birling engaged at the start of the play?
questions.explain: Sheila is engaged to Gerald Croft, son of a rival business family, Crofts Limited.
Eva Smith commits suicide by swallowing strong disinfectant, which burns her insides.

questions.q: What name did Eva Smith use when Gerald Croft met her at the Palace bar?
questions.explain: When Gerald met her she was calling herself Daisy Renton, and he made her his mistress.

questions.q: Why does Priestley have Mr Birling call the Titanic 'unsinkable' and dismiss talk of war?
options: To create dramatic irony, since the 1945 audience knows he is wrong
To show Birling is well-informed about world events
To foreshadow Birling's promotion to knighthood
To prove the Inspector is lying
questions.explain: The audience knows the Titanic sank and two world wars followed, so Birling's confident predictions expose him as foolish.

questions.q: What central message about responsibility does the Inspector deliver?
options: That we are all responsible for one another in society
That the poor must take responsibility for themselves
That only the government is responsible for the vulnerable
That responsibility belongs to individuals alone, not the community
questions.explain: The Inspector argues for collective social responsibility, insisting 'we are members of one body'.

questions.q: Why did Mr Birling dismiss Eva Smith from his factory?
options: She helped lead a strike asking for higher wages
She stole money from the office
She was rude to a customer
questions.explain: Birling sacked Eva as a ringleader after workers asked for a rise from 22 to 25 shillings a week.

questions.q: How did Sheila cause Eva Smith to lose her job at Milwards?
options: She complained out of jealousy and had her dismissed
She refused to work alongside her
questions.explain: Sheila, jealous when Eva suited a dress better, used her family's influence to have Eva sacked.

questions.q: What was Mrs Birling's role in Eva Smith's downfall?
options: She refused Eva help from the women's charity she chaired
She dismissed Eva from a shop
She reported Eva to the police
She evicted Eva from her lodgings
questions.explain: As chairwoman of the Brumley Women's Charity Organisation, Mrs Birling refused the pregnant Eva's appeal for support.

questions.q: What is significant about the play's cyclical ending?
options: A phone call announces a real inspector is coming to ask questions
The Inspector returns to arrest Mr Birling
Sheila leaves the family home for good
Eva Smith is revealed to be alive
questions.explain: The final phone call restarts events, trapping the unrepentant characters and reinforcing the play's warning.

questions.q: How do Priestley's own political beliefs shape the play?
options: As a socialist, he uses the Inspector to promote social equality
As a conservative, he defends the Birlings' wealth
As a pacifist, he condemns all forms of government
As a capitalist, he celebrates industrial success
questions.explain: Priestley was a socialist and channels his belief in collective responsibility through the Inspector's arguments.

questions.q: The Inspector warns that if people do not learn responsibility they will be taught it 'in fire and blood and anguish'. This most likely alludes to:
options: The two World Wars that followed 1912
A future factory fire in Brumley
questions.explain: The 1945 audience would recognise the phrase as pointing to the suffering of the World Wars the characters cannot foresee.

questions.q: Which characters most clearly represent Priestley's hope that the younger generation can change?
questions.explain: Sheila and Eric accept their guilt and are changed by the Inspector, unlike their unrepentant parents.

questions.q: The Inspector says there are 'millions and millions of Eva Smiths and John Smiths' still left. What does this suggest about class?
options: Eva stands for the many exploited working-class poor
There were literally millions of women named Eva Smith
The Birlings employed thousands of workers
The working class caused their own poverty
questions.explain: Eva becomes a symbol of the countless vulnerable working-class people harmed by the privileged.

questions.q: Which detail best supports the theme of gender and the vulnerability of women in 1912?
options: Eva depends on men like Gerald and Eric and has little power to protect herself
Mrs Birling votes in the general election
questions.explain: Eva's fate shows how working-class women in 1912 were economically and socially at the mercy of powerful men.

specSource: OCR GCSE (9–1) English Literature (J352) specification; An Inspector Calls
